_readme: Everything from the challenge's Resources tab (NASA_RESOURCES_PLAN.md, step N1), in one place. resources = each NASA (and CSA) resource: its name, its link, how the game uses it, the screens where the player sees it, and a sentence the Head Writer can copy into the submission form (shipped = true when that step is in the game). segments = NASA's four mission segments, shown as badges on the progress strip (step N2). cml = the Concept Maturity Level meter (step N2). glossary = the Space Dictionary words (step N7): word, meaning (20 words or fewer), real = one 'real missions do this' line, resource = which resource it comes from, unlock = when the stamp unlocks (scene = a screen id; category = a Design Room category; event = something the game reports). dictionary_bonus = the score points for a full set of stamps (DEFAULT: small bonus). Since UPGRADE_PLAN_V3 A2 (2026-11-14) the glossary is also the Q card file: pressing Q near something opens its entry (word, meaning, real, and a short source: link, or the resource's name). unlock { "event": "ask" } = the stamp unlocks only when you open its Q card (every card unlocks its stamp anyway). Which entry each thing points at: game_data.json hud > scene_questions, ship > station_questions, and GameState.question_for(). Every line has a real source or says PLACEHOLDER. Writers (Rena, Amy): every PLACEHOLDER below needs a check or a link before the final submission.
source_note: Links: found by web search (2026-11-14/15); a team member checks each one against the challenge's Resources tab. Kid meanings: written for the game (Head Writer checks them). Glossary sources: each word's source is the NASA resource named in its "resource" field (its link is in resources).

design_develop.name: Design and Develop Science Missions
design_develop.link: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20250002492 (NASA webinar deck, March 26 2025, Access to Space for All Systems Engineering series) (found by web search 2026-11-14: check it matches the challenge Resources tab)
design_develop.how_we_use: The game is split into NASA's four mission segments (launch, space, ground, user), shown as badges on the progress strip, and Review is the Verification step.
design_develop.submission_sentence: The game is split into NASA's four mission segments, shown on the progress strip.

cml.name: Concept Maturity Levels (CML)
cml.link: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20150007816 (Wessen, Borden, Ziemer, Kwok, 'Space Mission Concept Development Using Concept Maturity Levels', AIAA SPACE 2013); also https://science.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/03-ziemer-mission-development-101-cmls.pdf (found by web search 2026-11-14: check it matches the challenge Resources tab)
cml.how_we_use: A meter on the progress strip and the tablet levels the player's design up from CML 1 to CML 4.
cml.submission_sentence: The player's design levels up from CML 1 to CML 4.

mdl.name: Mission Design Lab (MDL)
mdl.link: https://etd.gsfc.nasa.gov/capabilities/integrated-design-center/mission-design-lab (found by web search 2026-11-14: check it matches the challenge Resources tab)
mdl.how_we_use: The Design Room is signposted Mission Design Lab, each part station is named for its discipline, hints are called Office Hours, and Review is an Equipment List.
mdl.submission_sentence: The design rooms are named for the MDL's disciplines, and Review is an equipment list.

telescope_game.name: A Learning Game About Telescopes
telescope_game.link: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/game-build-it-yourself/ (Build It Yourself: Satellite!, NASA Goddard) (found by web search 2026-11-14: check it matches the challenge Resources tab)
telescope_game.how_we_use: Options that cannot work for the chosen mission stand on dim pedestals with a reason, and the report matches the player to a real mission twin.
telescope_game.submission_sentence: Like this game, ours starts with the science goal and ends by matching you to a real mission.

cubesat_101.name: CubeSat 101
cubesat_101.link: https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/nasa_csli_cubesat_101_508.pdf (found by web search 2026-11-14: check it matches the challenge Resources tab)
cubesat_101.how_we_use: The Mission Briefing shows a ConOps picture strip, and each build minigame names the real step it stands for.
cubesat_101.submission_sentence: The briefing shows a ConOps, and each build minigame names the real step.

mission_viz.name: NASA Mission Viz
mission_viz.link: https://nasa.github.io/mission-viz (Web-based Space Mission Visualization) (found by web search 2026-11-14: check it matches the challenge Resources tab)
mission_viz.how_we_use: The trip map on the Bridge wall screen has three views like a mission viewer: whole trip, follow the ship, and destination (keys 1, 2, 3 on the ship).
mission_viz.submission_sentence: The Bridge trip map switches between whole-trip, follow-the-ship and destination views, like NASA's mission viewers.

gmat.name: GMAT (General Mission Analysis Tool)
gmat.link: https://software.nasa.gov/software/GSC-19640-1 (GMAT R2026 in the NASA Software Catalog); overview: https://etd.gsfc.nasa.gov/?p=18597 (found by web search 2026-11-14: check it matches the challenge Resources tab)
gmat.how_we_use: Named in a Did you know? in the orbit station. Nothing was installed; GMAT is desktop software and cannot run in a web game.
gmat.submission_sentence: The orbit station tells players that NASA plans real paths with GMAT.

vr_challenge.name: Visualize a Space Mission in VR (2023 challenge)
vr_challenge.how_we_use: Cited only: its checklist (concept, trajectory, timeline, 3D) matches the Bridge wall screen. No VR.

csa_games.name: CSA Digital Games and Activities
csa_games.link: https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/youth-educators/digital-games-and-activities.asp (found by web search 2026-11-14: check it matches the challenge Resources tab)
csa_games.how_we_use: Tone reference. One tip from the CSA site, once a writer adds it with its link (csa_tip below). Until then nothing shows in the game.
csa_games.submission_sentence: Tone reference, and the source of one in-game tip.

csa_tip._readme: One tip from the CSA Digital Games and Activities site, with its link. While text says PLACEHOLDER, the game does not show it. When filled, it shows as a Did you know? in the Mission Room.
csa_tip.text: The Canadian Space Agency has a game where you pick the spot on asteroid Bennu where the real OSIRIS-REx spacecraft grabbed its sample. Choosing the target well is step one of every mission!
csa_tip.link: https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/satellites/osiris-rex/activities/game.asp (from the CSA Digital Games and Activities page, found 2026-11-15)

segments._readme: NASA's four mission segments (Design and Develop Science Missions). Order matters: they light up in this order on the progress strip. scenes = which screens belong to the segment (the Design Room decides by category: rocket and orbit = launch, the rest = space).

ground.name: Ground segment
ground.meaning: The people and dishes on Earth

user.name: User segment
user.meaning: The scientists who use the data

segments.source: Segment names (launch, space, ground, user): Design and Develop Science Missions, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20250002492 (found by web search, check against the Resources tab). The scene grouping is a game-design choice.

cml._readme: The Concept Maturity Level meter. Each level turns on in order when its event happens (GameState.cml_events). nickname = our kid name (game-design choice). official_name = the name in the JPL paper: PLACEHOLDER until the Science & Data Lead copies it in. strip_scenes = the screens where the meter shows on the strip (it is about the design; the tablet always shows it).

Initial Feasibility (check: JPL CML paper, link in resources > cml)

levels.official_name: Trade Space (check: JPL CML paper, link in resources > cml)
levels.turns_on_when: The player changes a part after seeing the ripple effect

levels.official_name: Point Design (check: JPL CML paper, link in resources > cml)

cml.source: CML 1-4 names from JPL's Concept Maturity Levels paper: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20150007816; nicknames are ours (game-design choice).

dictionary_bonus._readme: DEFAULT (NASA_RESOURCES_PLAN.md N7): a full set of Space Dictionary stamps adds this many points to the report score (the total never goes over the maximum).
dictionary_bonus.source: Game-design choice (2026-11-14), waiting for the team's pass.

glossary.meaning: One trip with one science goal.
glossary.real: Every NASA mission starts by naming the question it will answer.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Something the mission must do or have to succeed.
glossary.real: NASA writes requirements before anyone designs a part.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: The whole mission plan, step by step, often drawn as pictures.
glossary.real: CubeSat 101 tells new teams to draw a ConOps first.
glossary.source: resource: cubesat_101 (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: The four big pieces: launch, space, ground and user.
glossary.real: NASA plans every science mission in these four segments.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Where a NASA team designs a whole mission together, fast.
glossary.real: Experts for power, heat, radio and more sit in one room.
glossary.source: resource: mdl (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: The rocket that carries your spacecraft to space.
glossary.real: NASA buys rides on rockets like the Falcon 9 and Atlas V.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: A path that loops around a planet or moon, again and again.
glossary.real: A lower orbit sees more detail but needs more fuel to reach.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: The path a spacecraft flies through space.
glossary.real: NASA plans trajectories with software like GMAT.
glossary.source: resource: gmat (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: The fuel a spacecraft burns to change speed.
glossary.real: Fuel is often the heaviest thing a spacecraft carries.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: The frame that holds every part together.
glossary.real: A structures engineer makes sure the frame survives launch.
glossary.source: resource: mdl (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Panels that turn sunlight into electricity.
glossary.real: In a planet's shadow, solar panels make no power at all.
glossary.source: resource: mdl (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Stores power for when there is no sunlight.
glossary.real: Spacecraft charge batteries in sunlight and use them in shadow.
glossary.source: resource: mdl (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Keeping the spacecraft pointed the right way.
glossary.real: Spinning wheels inside turn the spacecraft without fuel.
glossary.source: resource: mdl (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Keeping every part not too hot and not too cold.
glossary.real: Heaters warm parts in shade; radiators throw extra heat away.
glossary.source: resource: mdl (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Data sent from the spacecraft down to Earth.
glossary.real: A bigger dish antenna sends data home faster.
glossary.source: resource: mdl (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: The spacecraft's computer and electronics.
glossary.real: Space computers are built to survive radiation from the Sun.
glossary.source: resource: mdl (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: The science tools your spacecraft carries.
glossary.real: Everything else on a spacecraft exists to keep the payload working.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: One science tool, like a camera, a drill or a radar.
glossary.real: Each instrument needs power, mass and data from the spacecraft.
glossary.source: resource: telescope_game (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: How grown-up a mission idea is, from rough idea to real design.
glossary.real: JPL uses CML numbers to say how ready a mission idea is.
glossary.source: resource: cml (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Checking that the design really meets every requirement.
glossary.real: NASA verifies a design before it is built and flown.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Every part with its mass, power and cost, added up.
glossary.real: Mission design teams keep a running equipment list.
glossary.source: resource: mdl (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Putting all the parts together into one spacecraft.
glossary.real: Real teams integrate and test parts step by step.
glossary.source: resource: cubesat_101 (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Shaking a spacecraft hard, to be sure nothing falls off at launch.
glossary.real: Spacecraft are shaken on test tables before launch.
glossary.source: resource: cubesat_101 (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Loading propellant into the tanks, carefully, before launch.
glossary.real: Fueling is one of the last jobs before launch.
glossary.source: resource: cubesat_101 (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Every team says 'go' or 'no go' right before launch.
glossary.real: The launch director asks each team, one by one.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Dropping an empty rocket part so the rest flies lighter.
glossary.real: Most rockets drop their first stage a few minutes after liftoff.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: The long, quiet flight between planets.
glossary.real: During cruise, teams check every system and fix small problems.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Radio messages take time to cross space.
glossary.real: A radio command takes minutes to reach Mars.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: Big dishes on Earth that talk to spacecraft.
glossary.real: NASA's Deep Space Network has big dishes around the world.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: The scientists who use the data a mission sends home.
glossary.real: Mission data is shared so scientists everywhere can study it.
glossary.source: resource: design_develop (see its link in resources)

glossary.meaning: A jar of peanuts JPL teams open before big mission moments, just for luck.
glossary.real: The tradition began with the Ranger 7 Moon mission in 1964.
glossary.source: https://science.nasa.gov/missions/what-are-jpls-lucky-peanuts/ (Ranger 7, July 28 1964)

glossary.meaning: A small plush toy. When it starts to float, the crew knows they are weightless.
glossary.real: Artemis II flew a plush mascot named Rise as its zero-g indicator.
glossary.source: https://www.nasa.gov/general/moonmascot/ (Artemis II mascot Rise); also https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/cosmonaut-oleg-novitskiy-holds-up-zero-g-indicator/

glossary.meaning: All the money the mission may spend, the rocket included.
glossary.real: NASA's MAVEN Mars orbiter cost $671 million over its whole life.
glossary.source: MAVEN press kit, Quick Facts p. 4: https://mars.nasa.gov/files/resources/MAVEN_PressKit_Final.pdf

glossary.meaning: How heavy everything is. Your rocket must be able to lift it all.
glossary.real: MRO weighed 2,180 kg at launch, and 1,149 kg of that was fuel.
glossary.source: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=2005-029A

glossary.meaning: Electricity: what the solar panels make, minus what the parts use.
glossary.real: Dust on its solar panels slowly took InSight's power until it stopped in 2022.
glossary.source: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/insight/nasa-retires-insight-mars-lander-mission-after-years-of-science/

glossary.meaning: How fast the radio can send data home to Earth.
glossary.real: MRO was built to send about 600 kilobits per second, even with Mars far away.
glossary.source: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mro-launch-Aug05.pdf

glossary.meaning: How much science your instruments collect each day.
glossary.real: MRO's HiRISE camera sent home more than 12 terabits in its first two years.
glossary.source: https://boris.unibe.ch/25369/1/2005JE002605.pdf

glossary.meaning: How many months the spacecraft must keep working.
glossary.real: MRO's main science phase ran two years, November 2006 to December 2008.
glossary.source: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mro-launch-Aug05.pdf

glossary.meaning: Earth's moon. A spacecraft can get there in about three days.
glossary.real: Apollo astronauts left seismometers that recorded moonquakes until 1977.
glossary.source: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/experiment/display.action?id=1971-063C-01; 3 days: Apollo 8, https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/smd/how-long-does-it-take-to-get-to-the-moon-mars-jupiter-we-asked-a-nasa-expert-episode-51/

glossary.meaning: The red planet. The trip takes about seven months.
glossary.real: In 2008 the Phoenix lander dug up real water ice near Mars's north pole.
glossary.source: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-phoenix-mars-lander-confirms-frozen-water/; 7 months: MRO 210 days, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=2005-029A

glossary.meaning: The hottest planet, wrapped in thick clouds. Nobody lands there.
glossary.real: Its surface is about 467 °C, hot enough to melt lead.
glossary.source: https://science.nasa.gov/venus/venus-facts/

glossary.meaning: A SpaceX rocket. Its first stage lands and flies again.
glossary.real: NASA's PACE Earth science satellite launched on a Falcon 9.
glossary.source: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-awards-launch-services-contract-for-earth-science-mission/

glossary.meaning: A ULA rocket with no strap-on boosters.
glossary.real: NASA's Lucy asteroid mission launched on an Atlas V 401.
glossary.source: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-awards-launch-services-contract-for-lucy-mission/

glossary.meaning: A bigger Atlas V with four strap-on boosters, for heavy loads.
glossary.real: It launched the Mars 2020 mission with the Perseverance rover.
glossary.source: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-awards-launch-services-contract-for-mars-2020-rover-mission/

glossary.meaning: The days when a rocket can leave and reach its target using the least fuel.
glossary.real: Earth and Mars line up for a good launch only about every 26 months.
glossary.source: https://mars.nasa.gov/msl/timeline/launch/launch-windows/

_real_things_readme: UPGRADE_PLAN_V3 C1: one file for the real things. real_missions, real_rockets and astronaut_facts: every entry has name, year, one sentence, a source link, and shows_in (where it shows in the game: a glossary id = that Q card, school_<resource> = that Mission School beat, intro = the intro plaques, flight_<mission> = the flight log line at the end of the trip, mission_room / briefing / twin = text that lives in story.json or destinations.json). An entry whose status or source says PLACEHOLDER does not ship (GameState.is_checked). Section 4 rules: facts only, never invented dialogue, no photos. Astronaut facts checked by web search on NASA pages, 2026-11-14 (the Science & Data Lead re-checks each link).

real_missions.name: Apollo 8
real_missions.sentence: Apollo 8 took just under three days to get from Earth orbit to orbit around the Moon.
real_missions.flight_log_line: Day {day}: Apollo 8 took just under three days to reach the Moon. We made it in about the same.

real_missions.name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
real_missions.sentence: MRO launched in August 2005 and reached Mars orbit 210 days later.
real_missions.flight_log_line: Day {day}: MRO took 210 days to reach Mars. Our trip is built on its real one.

real_missions.name: Pioneer Venus Orbiter
real_missions.sentence: Pioneer Venus launched in May 1978 and entered Venus orbit 198 days later.
real_missions.flight_log_line: Day {day}: Pioneer Venus took 198 days to reach Venus. Our trip is built on its real one.

real_missions.name: Apollo 11 seismometer
real_missions.sentence: Apollo 11 left the first seismometer on the Moon; it felt moonquakes.

real_missions.name: Phoenix lander
real_missions.sentence: Phoenix dug into the soil near Mars's north pole and found water ice.

real_missions.name: Magellan
real_missions.sentence: Magellan mapped about 98% of Venus with radar, right through the clouds.

real_missions.name: VEGA balloons
real_missions.sentence: Two Soviet VEGA balloons floated in the clouds of Venus.

real_rockets.name: Falcon 9
real_rockets.sentence: A Falcon 9 launched NASA's PACE Earth science satellite.

real_rockets.name: Atlas V 401
real_rockets.sentence: An Atlas V 401 launched NASA's Lucy asteroid mission.

real_rockets.name: Atlas V 541
real_rockets.sentence: An Atlas V 541 launched Mars 2020 with the Perseverance rover.

astronaut_facts.name: Buzz Aldrin
astronaut_facts.sentence: Set up the first seismometer on the Moon.

astronaut_facts.name: David Scott
astronaut_facts.sentence: Drilled holes for the heat flow probes; the hard ground stopped him at about 1.6 m.

astronaut_facts.name: Scott Kelly
astronaut_facts.sentence: Lived 340 days on the space station so doctors could study long trips.

astronaut_facts.name: Christina Koch
astronaut_facts.sentence: Spent 328 days in space in one trip, the longest single flight by a woman.

astronaut_facts.name: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, Jeremy Hansen
astronaut_facts.sentence: Flew around the Moon in April 2026, farther from Earth than any people before.

astronaut_facts.name: STS-30 crew (Space Shuttle Atlantis)
astronaut_facts.sentence: Released Magellan, the first planetary probe launched from a Space Shuttle.

intro_plaques._enabled_readme: 2026-11-15 team note: the plaques felt out of place in the intro, and the real astronauts now meet you on the ship (data/crew.json). enabled = false turns them off; true brings them back.
intro_plaques._readme: UPGRADE_PLAN_V3 C4: the name plaques in the intro (text only, no photos). names = the plaque lines; line = what the General says about them (he is our own character; the real people never speak). Both come from the checked astronaut_facts above.
intro_plaques.line: Real crews set up seismometers on the Moon. In 2026, Artemis II flew all the way around it.
intro_plaques.speaker: General
intro_plaques._timing_readme: at_seconds = when the intro pauses for the plaques (just before "You. I want you." at 18.2 s); show_seconds = how long they stay. Game-design choice.

did_you_know: The Did you know? tips stay in data/story.json ("did_you_know"), each with its own NASA source. The Design Room shows the tip for each category after you preview an option (rule 1: do, then learn).
